item.title: Art Deco in the Outback
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
There is a striking visual dissonance that occurs when you look through a frame of polished timber and brushed brass onto three hundred miles of unvarnished red dirt. Inside the carriage, the lines are clean, curved, and disciplined—the geometry of Art Deco, quieted by the tactile warmth of saddle leather, decorative timber, and fine sheepskin. Outside, the landscape is sprawling, wind-scoured, and indifferent to human geometry.

To the untrained eye, Art Deco and the Australian Outback might seem like awkward bedfellows: an urban, European design movement dropped into the silica dust of the Red Center. But in Australia, these two forces share an intimate, historical alliance. Understanding that relationship is the secret to understanding why long-distance rail travel across this continent remains one of the world’s most evocative cultural passages.

The Interwar Frontier: Modernism in Red Dirt

In the 1920s and 1930s, Australia was experiencing an extraordinary industrial and pastoral boom. Wealth flowed directly out of the ground—driven by wool clip, wheat harvests, cattle drives, and rich veins of gold. As transcontinental rail tracks were laid to stitch isolated inland settlements to coastal ports, a distinct architectural wave followed the iron rails inward.

When Art Deco arrived from Paris and Hollywood, remote frontier towns embraced it with fierce pride. Streamlined, curve-cornered pubs, civic halls, and railway stations built from rendered brick, vitrolite glass, and terrazzo sprang up in dusty mining and pastoral outposts like Kalgoorlie and Broken Hill. These structures were more than shelter; they were bold monuments to modern ambition—physical declarations that culture, elegance, and connectivity had arrived on the edge of the wilderness.

Tactile Storytelling Onboard

That historical interwar spirit finds its modern rebirth aboard Journey Beyond’s Aurora Australis Suites aboard the Indian Pacific and The Ghan. Designed by Woods Bagot, the carriages deliberately step away from generic modern minimalism to embrace an artisanal, heritage-driven palette.

The materials chosen for the interiors—smooth timber veneers, sculpted stone surfaces, tactile sheepskin, and rich leather—are direct nods to the pastoral commodities that built the nation’s interior economy. These are the textures of the drovers, wool merchants, and railway builders who shaped Australia’s early cross-continental trade.

“The luxury interiors are characterised by an artisanal, heritage-driven approach to detail and meticulous craftsmanship. Featuring a palette of decorative timber, stone surfaces, and accents of sheepskin and leather, the interiors create a rich and layered experience that reflects both heritage and landscape.”

— Rosina Di Maria, Director at Woods Bagot

Paired with private butler service, curated regional dining featuring Kangaroo Island lobster and premium Wagyu, and Champagne Bollinger served in crystal glass, the suite becomes a living capsule. It honors the interwar golden age of rail travel without feeling like a museum piece.

Overlapping Timelines: From Gold Mines to Sacred Waterholes

As the train cuts its steady path across the continent, the real power of the journey reveals itself in the layer cake of history visible outside the window. The rail line acts as a moving corridor connecting three distinct temporal scales:

1. Modern Pastoral & Industrial Heritage: At Kalgoorlie in Western Australia, passengers step off into the legacy of Paddy Hannan’s 1893 gold rush, exploring historic sites before soaring over the vast pit of the mining frontier. In the Adelaide Hills, the train pauses near stone winemaking estates established during the same interwar period.

2. Deep Geological Time & First Nations Memory: When The Ghan pauses at Katherine or Alice Springs, guests take to the sky by helicopter or plane to reach Nitmiluk Gorge and Uluru. Here, the polished lines of the train yield to 13 deep sandstone gorges carved by ancient rivers and sacred monoliths carrying tens of thousands of years of First Nations songlines and rock art around Mutitjulu Waterhole.

3. The Cadence of the Present: Inside the carriage, travelers observe both timelines passing in slow motion—paying the price of distance in time rather than flying blind over the continent’s immense heart.

The Story Continues

Rail travel remains unmatched in its ability to tell complex stories of place. By marrying the geometric elegance of Art Deco craftsmanship with the unyielding majesty of the outback, journeys like The Ghan and the Indian Pacific do not merely carry passengers across geography. They transport them through overlapping eras—proving that on the rails, the story of Australian heritage continues to unfold with every passing mile.

item.title: The Algarve After Summer
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Autumn brings a different rhythm to Portugal’s Algarve, where warm days, golden coastlines and fewer crowds make the season particularly appealing for a coastal escape. At W Algarve in Albufeira, the change of season is an invitation to spend more time outdoors, from exploring the region’s dramatic cliffs to getting out on the water.

The hotel’s Whatever/Whenever service can arrange experiences that take advantage of the landscape, including coasteering and cliff jumping, private kayak excursions into the Benagil caves, and surfing lessons along the Algarve coast. Closer to the hotel, Evaristo and Castelo beaches offer a quieter way to experience the shoreline, with scenic cliff walks and broad views over the Atlantic. Back at the resort, newly added padel, pickleball and tennis courts bring another dimension to an active autumn stay.

The Curated Take: The Algarve is at its most interesting when the intensity of summer begins to ease. Autumn makes room for a more leisurely relationship with the coast, whether that means exploring its caves and cliffs, walking between beaches or lingering outdoors without the pressure of peak-season crowds. W Algarve provides a contemporary base for experiencing that quieter side of southern Portugal.

item.title: A Taste of Spain Above Bangkok
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Three years after opening in Bangkok’s On Nut neighborhood, INNSiDE by Meliá Bangkok Sukhumvit is marking the occasion by leaning into one of its most distinctive features: the skyline. Rising 34 floors above the city, the 208-room hotel combines contemporary design with a distinctly Spanish influence, culminating in LUZ Bangkok Tapas Bar on the 33rd floor and a transparent infinity pool directly overhead.

The hotel’s “Feel the Skyline Vibes” experience brings that combination together through Spanish tapas, cocktails and a sunset cocktail-making class overlooking Bangkok. At LUZ, guests can sample tapas, Spanish wines, cocktails and signature sangrias under the direction of Spanish Chef de Cuisine Juan Ignacio García Racionero, known as Chef Nacho. The restaurant’s position beneath the transparent pool creates one of the property’s more unusual visual moments, while the 34th-floor pool provides another perspective on the city. The hotel also incorporates co-working spaces, giving the property a distinctly contemporary take on the urban hotel.

The Curated Take: LUZ gives INNSiDE Bangkok a particularly interesting identity. Rather than simply adding a rooftop bar to a city hotel, the property has created a vertical experience where Spanish food and hospitality meet Bangkok’s skyline. It is a reminder that a sense of place in a city hotel doesn’t necessarily mean reproducing the destination literally. Sometimes it comes from the unexpected conversation between two cultures.

item.title: Las Ventanas al Paraíso Captures the Soul of Southern Baja
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Las Ventanas al Paraíso, A Rosewood Resort has earned a place among the world’s leading hotels, ranking No. 25 on The 50 Best Hotels 2026 list. The Los Cabos resort also received the WhistlePig Highest Climber Award after moving up 19 places from its No. 44 position in 2025, marking its second consecutive year on the global ranking.

Set along the coast of Southern Baja, Las Ventanas is designed around the meeting of desert and sea, with Mexican artistry and regional craftsmanship woven throughout its 84 suites and villas. Five restaurants and bars draw on the produce and flavors of the region, while the resort’s experiences range from horseback riding along the beach and healing rituals at its spa to sunrise yoga and time spent beside its eight pools. The property also offers 30 Rosewood Residences, including the distinctive Ty Warner Mansion.

The 2026 ranking was compiled from votes by more than 800 members of The 50 Best Hotels Academy, comprising hoteliers, travel journalists, educators and experienced luxury travelers. For Las Ventanas, the recognition reinforces a hospitality philosophy centered not simply on luxury, but on creating a strong connection to the landscape, culture and craftsmanship of Southern Baja.

The Curated Take: Las Ventanas works because its luxury is deeply tied to where it is. The resort doesn’t need to manufacture a sense of place when the contrast between the Baja desert and the Sea of Cortez is already so distinctive. Mexican art, local craftsmanship, regional cuisine and experiences rooted in the landscape give the property an identity that extends well beyond its accommodations.

item.title: Capella Sydney Puts Heritage at the Heart of Modern Luxury
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Capella Sydney has once again earned a place among the world’s leading hotels, ranking No. 16 in The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026 and receiving the designation of Best Hotel in Oceania. The recognition comes less than four years after the property opened in 2023, bringing international attention to a hotel whose identity is closely tied to one of Sydney’s most significant heritage buildings.

Set within the restored former Department of Education building in Sydney’s Sandstone Precinct, the 192-room Capella combines the structure’s original architecture with contemporary interiors and a collection of more than 1,400 artworks. Its spaces extend from Auriga Spa and a 20-metre heated pool to Brasserie 1930, McRae Bar and Aperture, creating a hotel experience that is as much about culture and design as it is about accommodation. Its location also places guests within easy reach of Sydney Harbour, the Opera House and Harbour Bridge.

The 2026 recognition was determined by votes from more than 800 members of The 50 Best Hotels Academy, a group comprising hoteliers, travel journalists, educators and experienced luxury travelers. Capella Sydney was also named No. 12 and Best Hotel in Oceania in the 2025 ranking.

The Curated Take: Capella Sydney demonstrates how heritage can become an active part of a contemporary hotel rather than simply a backdrop. The restoration gives the property an architectural connection to Sydney, while its art, dining and wellness spaces create additional ways for guests to engage with the city. For travelers drawn to hotels with a strong sense of place, that combination is arguably more interesting than the ranking itself.

item.title: Lafayette’s Fall Season Gets a National Spotlight
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Lafayette, Louisiana, is having a moment as a fall destination. The heart of Acadiana placed fifth in the 2026 USA TODAY 10Best Readers’ Choice Awards for Best Place to Visit for Fall, following four weeks of public voting after being selected as one of 20 destinations nominated by a panel of travel experts.

The recognition puts a national spotlight on the elements that make autumn distinctive in Lafayette and the surrounding Acadiana region, from a calendar of fall festivals to the area’s deeply rooted culinary traditions, outdoor experiences and distinctive Cajun and Creole culture. This marks the third consecutive year Lafayette has been nominated and named among USA TODAY’s 10Best fall destinations, suggesting that its appeal extends well beyond the traditional peak travel seasons.

The Curated Take: Lafayette’s fall appeal is less about seasonal scenery than about what happens on the ground. Festivals, food and cultural traditions give the season a sense of occasion, while the region’s outdoor experiences provide another way to explore Acadiana. For travelers looking for a destination where autumn is expressed through community and culture rather than simply changing leaves, Lafayette offers a distinctly Louisiana interpretation of the season.

item.title: Highways from the Silver Screen
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Seven iconic cinematic routes, from coastal backroads to cross-country detours.

There is a distinct geometry to the cinematic road trip. Long before turn-by-turn navigation smoothed over the friction of transit, putting characters on the open road forced them to confront raw distance, shifting topography, and each other. Unlike air travel, which erases the world between point A and point B, the road trip honors the transition. Across these seven journeys, the route itself becomes as essential to the narrative as the travelers behind the wheel.

For some, the road is a stage for family dynamics testing their limits across state lines. In National Lampoon’s Vacation, Clark Griswold herds his family from Chicago to Anaheim in a station wagon along Interstate 40 and historic Route 66. The journey’s defining visual remains the dusty, sprawling expanse of Monument Valley along the Utah-Arizona border—a magnificent backdrop that contrasts sharply with their chaotic trek toward the locked gates of Walley World. Decades later, Little Miss Sunshine traced a similar western path along Interstate 10, carrying the fractured Hoover family from Albuquerque to Redondo Beach in a sputtering 1971 Volkswagen Microbus. The film’s most memorable stretch unfolds on the highway shoulder, where the family must run alongside the moving bus to jump through the sliding door—a physical manifestation of keeping a family moving forward despite mechanical failure.

In lighter territory, the road serves as the ultimate test of directional sense. Dumb and Dumber tracks an absurd cross-country haul from Providence, Rhode Island, to Aspen, Colorado. Its defining highway moment arrives when a wrong turn in Nebraska sends Lloyd and Harry driving for hours in the wrong direction across the freezing plains toward Kansas on a tiny moped—a hilarious, cautionary reminder of what happens when you abandon the map entirely.

For others, the highway provides space for quiet reflection and unexpected bonding. In Sideways, two friends take a battered Saab convertible from San Diego into the backroads of Santa Barbara County’s Santa Ynez Valley. Cruising along Foxen Canyon Road past golden, oak-studded hills and rolling vineyards, the landscape mirrors the slow pace of wine country and the quiet existential reckonings of midlife. Further east, Rain Man takes a deliberate detour as Charlie Babbitt drives his autistic savant brother, Raymond, from Cincinnati to Los Angeles in a 1949 Buick Roadmaster. By intentionally avoiding interstates for two-lane state highways and Route 66, the slow pace of the open road forces Charlie to adapt to Raymond’s unhurried rhythm, transforming a hostile drive into genuine connection.

The road also acts as a moving sanctuary for those seeking identity or escape. In Almost Famous, a young journalist joins the rock band Stillwater aboard their tour bus, “Doris,” tracing a hazy arc through the American Rust Belt and Midwest. The heart of the film rests in a late-night drive down a dark highway after a chaotic party, where the entire bus quietly sings along to Elton John’s “Tiny Dancer,” capturing the fleeting, sacred unity found only in transit.

At the far end of the spectrum, Into the Wild follows Christopher McCandless from Atlanta through the Southwest and Pacific Northwest, ending in the Alaskan interior. The journey culminates on the desolate, snow-dusted stretch of the Stampede Trail near Healy, Alaska, where the gravel peters out into pure wilderness—marking the final transition from the highway to complete isolation.

Whether navigating family chaos, rolling vineyards, or distant horizons, these seven films remind us of a fundamental travel truth: the moments that define a trip rarely happen at the destination—they happen along the way.

item.title: The Journey to the World’s Northernmost Commercial Lodge
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Nordenskiöld Lodge, reaching the destination is part of the experience. Set within the Arctic landscape of Spitsbergen, the remote lodge is the northernmost commercial lodge in the world and can only be reached by boat or snowmobile. In winter, Basecamp Explorer’s Glacier Odyssey turns the journey into a 100-kilometer expedition across snowy terrain, glaciers, frozen fjords and wind-carved valleys.

The lodge itself offers a striking contrast to the surrounding wilderness. Designed by Norwegian interior expert Halvor Bakke, its warm materials and colors frame views of the glacier, mountains and fjord, creating an intimate retreat within an otherwise immense landscape. After days spent crossing the Arctic by snowmobile, evenings center on communal dinners and time around the fire with the lodge host, sharing stories and knowledge of the region.

The Curated Take: Nordenskiöld Lodge is compelling because the Arctic isn’t simply scenery surrounding the hotel. The remoteness defines the experience from beginning to end. The 100-kilometer snowmobile journey makes arrival feel earned, while the lodge provides just enough warmth and intimacy to create a meaningful counterpoint to the wilderness outside.

item.title: A Winter Escape Where the Water Runs Warm
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers ready to leave winter behind entirely, Rio Perdido Hotel & Thermal River offers a very different kind of seasonal escape. Set within a wilderness landscape in Costa Rica’s Guanacaste region, the eco-luxury retreat combines outdoor adventure with the natural thermal waters of the volcanic landscape.

Days can move between hiking and mountain biking and experiences centered on the property’s thermal rivers and mineral pools, with volcanic mud adding another dimension to the retreat’s connection to the surrounding geology. Winter is particularly well suited to a Costa Rica escape, as the country’s dry season generally runs from mid-December through late April, bringing warm, sunny conditions to the outdoor landscape.

The Curated Take: Rio Perdido’s appeal is that wellness here begins with the landscape itself. Rather than separating adventure from relaxation, the retreat makes the volcanic environment the common thread, allowing travelers to move from an active day outdoors to naturally warm waters without leaving the setting that makes Guanacaste distinctive.

item.title: Valletta Offers a Warmer Take on the European Winter City Break
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
While Europe’s best-known winter city breaks tend to revolve around colder capitals and Christmas markets, Valletta offers a distinctly Mediterranean alternative. Malta’s capital combines mild winter weather with UNESCO-listed architecture, centuries of history, a growing culinary scene and a festive calendar that gives travelers plenty of reasons to explore beyond the summer season.

Iniala Valletta provides a particularly well-positioned base for experiencing the city. The hotel has introduced Solis, a collection of suites overlooking the Grand Harbour, while its two-MICHELIN-starred ION Harbour has recently been refurbished and a new dining concept, Anaalā, has joined the property’s culinary offering. The hotel’s winter programming also includes cultural, gastronomic and adventure experiences, including private access to St John’s Co-Cathedral. With fewer summer crowds, travelers can spend their days wandering Valletta’s historic streets, exploring the coast and venturing into surrounding towns at a more leisurely pace.

The Curated Take: Valletta makes sense as a winter destination precisely because it doesn’t try to recreate the traditional European winter city break. Its appeal is the combination of history, architecture, food and Mediterranean light, with winter offering a chance to experience one of Europe’s most atmospheric capitals without the intensity of its summer season.
